articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source Taiwan has blocked the websites of Coinbase Global Inc. and Kalshi Inc. over suspected election betting, weeks before local polls that will test support for President Lai Ching-te’s government. A New Taipei court authorized the Taiwanese communications regulator and internet registry to bar domestic access to the platforms, according to a ruling seen by Bloomberg News. Some Coinbase users in Taiwan reported being unable to access the site since Wednesday. The Criminal Investigation Bureau, which sought the order, said in response to questions from Bloomberg that the websites were suspected of violating the Public Officials Election and Recall Act. The law prohibits operating gambling for profit based on the outcome of an election or recall. Coinbase and Kalshi didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The bureau said it requested the restrictions to protect election integrity and prevent “overseas interference,” without giving further details. Taiwanese authorities have separately warned that money from mainland China could enter the island through underground financial channels and be used to influence elections. The government has stepped up scrutiny of illicit financial flows ahead of the Nov. 28 vote, including underground gambling operations. Requests for proposals are another lever agencies lean on in the acquisition process to assess options and evaluate approaches.  But the rise of generative AI has complicated the efforts, according to Anil Chaudhry, senior advisor for AI, autonomy and national security for the Department of Transportation.  “We used to get maybe 10 responses to an RFI or RFP,” Chaudhry said Wednesday onstage during the SAP Public Sector Summit in Washington, D.C. “Now, we’re getting 500 because everybody puts it in a chatbot and sends it to us.” Agencies are finding it challenging to sift through it all.  “Everybody in government has these issues where they’re getting overwhelmed by qualitative information,” Chaudhry said. “Trying to deal with that volume, it’s a whole-of-government problem, and we have whole-of-government teams working on these problems.”  Private-sector companies are overflowing with generative AI tools that produce lengthy, oftentimes glib chunks of texts. Vendors have even begun catering to companies that want to speed up the response process.  InspectMind, for example, has a new product that is marketed as a system that can easily create first drafts for RFI responses. Nomic touts an AI agent that drafts RFI responses, reducing time spent on the task. Datagrid is another AI vendor looking to capitalize on the growing market.  While industry has created the influx, it could also aid agencies in scrutinizing the large volume of content.  In a recent RFI , Immigration and Customs Enforcement asked interested vendors to help the Department of Homeland Security component identify methods that would distinguish qualified suitors from AI slop.  “The Government recognizes that the proliferation of generative AI tools has made it easier to produce highly polished, technically accurate written proposals,” ICE said in its request to industry. “To ensure the Government selects a vendor with genuine, proven capabilities to execute the scope of work, what specific evaluation methods… do you recommend to differentiate genuine, demonstrated hands-on capability features creation from purely generative AI responses?” Combatting AI with more AI is on the table, too.  Earlier this year, a Defense Department request for proposals included a disclosure of potential AI use in the review process.  “The Government may employ AI as a tool to assist in the analysis and review of offeror proposals,” DOD said in accompanying documents, pointing to a variety of use cases, such as summarizing proposal content, identifying compliance with requirements, and highlighting areas of potential strength, weakness, or risk. “Notwithstanding the use of AI tools to support the evaluation process, all final evaluation judgements and source selection decisions will be made exclusively by duly appointed Government personnel,” the agency added.  The strategy has been met with some skepticism from lawyers and stakeholders.  “It is not difficult to imagine the potential for generative AI tools to hallucinate or otherwise mischaracterize proposal details that are material to an agency’s award decision,” Michael Brewer, a member of Burr and Forman’s construction practice group, said in an April blog post .

articles.title: Mercenary Malware Delivered via Targeted Ads
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app. The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025. A clear warning signal “This investigation should … serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.” The ads were provided by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that brands itself as a legitimate advertising company, but Citizen Lab said it operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners. The company acts as a broker between parties that want to display their ads and publishers or app makers that seek revenue in return for showing them. In this capacity, Discover-Tech acts as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem,” a role that appears to be “Discover-Tech’s primary purpose,” Citizen Lab said. The brokering involves a bidding process in which advertisers offer a fee in exchange for their ads appearing on the devices of individuals in particular demographics. Using users’ unique mobile ID, location, IP address, and other breadcrumbs, the brokers are able to assemble detailed profiles of millions of people. Citizen Lab said it obtained more than 4 billion bidding records handled by Discover-Tech. They revealed that Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June 2026. Among the major vendors that listed Discover-Tech as a “certified” or “verified” vendor were Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe. The Israeli firm also used European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union. Discover-Tech has served ads through major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Google and IAB Europe have since removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries, and Google further terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms. Beeswax has removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform. Fellow ad platform Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains. Thursday’s report said that Discover-Tech ad impressions have appeared on government and national-security-linked networks throughout the world: NATO, United Nations networks, European lawmaking bodies, critical infrastructure providers in Australia, and armed forces and government agencies in Norway and Sweden. “Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report,” Citizen Lab said. The research lab said that the mercenary malware installed through AdFection was developed and distributed by Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”). Under the arrangement with Discover-Tech, targets with specific profiles of interest to the Candiru customers received ads that carried JavaScript or other code that connected to Candiru’s control servers. In response, those servers delivered an exploit that served the zero-click payload when the ad appeared on an individual’s device. The research doesn’t describe the vulnerabilities exploited in the zero-click attacks or the final malware that was installed in them. It’s likely they were zero-days that have been fixed after Citizen Lab discovered the campaign. Citizen Lab didn’t immediately respond to questions. Messages sent to Discover-Tech and Candiru went unanswered. Citizen Lab called on advertisers and government officials to take concrete action to proactively prevent campaigns like AdFection. Beyond that, users can reduce the risk of being infected by installing ad blockers, resetting mobile advertising ID in iOS and Android settings (it’s unclear why the researchers didn’t advise turning off personalized ads altogether), and installing ad-blocking software on home or office networks. As always, installing updates in a timely manner is also a must. Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. articles.title: Anthropic PAC Spends Quarter Million Lobbying DC
articles.content: Anthropic’s PAC spent more than $250K in third quarter, splitting between parties by Miranda Nazzaro - 10/15/26 12:03 PM ET Link copied - 10/15/26 12:03 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING Anthropic’s corporate political action committee poured $161,000 into campaigns across the aisle last month, bringing their total third-quarter spending to more than $250,000, according to spending records first shared with The Hill. The employee-funded PAC, AnthroPAC, spent more than $255,000 across the third quarter, marking the artificial intelligence firm’s latest push for political clout in Washington. The party breakdown for Anthropic’s total third-quarter contributions was 50.6 percent for Republicans and 49.4 percent for Democrats. Overall, AnthroPAC spent $130,000 on Republican campaigns and $125,500 on Democrats in the third quarter, according to spending records obtained by The Hill ahead of the monthly federal filing deadline next Tuesday. September was the company’s biggest month for spending as the midterm election approaches. About $77,000 was spent in August, and $17,500 in July. Recipients of the political donations include the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and various party-affiliated PACs. Some of the GOP donation recipients include Sens. Mike Rounds (S.D.), Kevin Cramer (N.D.), Kevin Hern (Okla.), Jon Husted (Ohio) and Ashley Moody (Fla.), along with Reps. Lisa McClain (Mich.), Laurel Lee (Fla.), Brian Mast (Fla.), Rob Wittman (Va.) and Tom Emmer (Minn.). Mike Rogers, who is running for a Senate seat in Michigan, also received donation funds. Democratic recipients include Sens. Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Alex Padilla (Calif.), Chris Coons (Del.) and Mark Warner (Va.). Anthropic launched the employee-funded PAC in April, and it is overseen by a bipartisan board. The donations are capped at $5,000 per person per year under federal law and will be publicly reported through Federal Election Commission filings. Other technology companies such as Nvidia , Google, Microsoft and Amazon have similarly structured PACs.  Shortly after the PAC’s launch, a handful of figures in President Trump’s orbit  expressed skepticism Friday that it would donate to both sides given Anthropic’s rocky relationship with the Trump administration and past donations to Democrats.  Anthropic cannot contribute directly to the PAC, but it has thrown money into other political initiatives this year. This included $40 million to Public First Action, a group launched last year to support efforts to develop AI safeguards.  Anthropic clashed with the Trump administration earlier this year over its push for AI safeguards. The Pentagon took the unprecedented move in February to label Anthropic a supply chain risk after the company demanded its technology not be used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans.  Anthropic sued the Pentagon in California and Washington, D.C., arguing the agency retaliated against the AI firm for what it believes is a “protected viewpoint” of the company. A federal judge in California ruled the blacklist was illegal and that it violated the First Amendment and due process clause of the Fifth Amendment. A three-judge panel at the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals sided with the Trump administration, setting the stage for a potential Supreme Court fight. Earlier this week, Anthropic asked the appeals court to reconsider their decision. articles.title: Gen-AI Hacks: Companies Aren't Paying for Damages
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents . The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7. Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.” Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group , rather than a direct hacking victim. AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities. Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties . When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd , to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.) “This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.” Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs. Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.” Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes. Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge , whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive. This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter . Read previous newsletters here.

articles.content: Advertisement The OpenAI engineer who was charged this week with planting a secret recording device at the artificial intelligence company recently said he helped advise government agencies in Saudi Arabia on technology, and was listed as a partner at a venture capital firm alongside a member of the Saudi royal family. In an Arabic podcast interview last month, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, said he and other Saudi tech professionals in Silicon Valley had formed a group that advised Saudi organisations, including the kingdom’s social insurance agency. Separately, RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, lists Alfozan as a venture partner on its website, along with Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud. Abdulrahman Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. Instagram Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. He was an engineer at Meta before joining a startup that went through Y Combinator, the Silicon Valley startup accelerator. He gained permanent residency status in the United States in 2020, according to court documents, and was hired by OpenAI in July 2025. Details about Alfozan are emerging after OpenAI disclosed earlier this week that it had discovered a hidden recording device in a conference room in one of its San Francisco buildings. The company said it had traced the device to Alfozan, who was arrested by the FBI and charged with trying to secretly record conversations using an electronic device. Advertisement The incident has fuelled concerns about the security of leading AI labs like OpenAI that create advanced AI models that are among the most closely guarded secrets in the US technology industry. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said that what had happened at OpenAI underscored how winning the AI race “is a national security prerogative.” An image released by the US Department of Justice appears to show Abdulrahman Alfozan behind the TV where a bug was hidden. US Department of Justice OpenAI said Alfozan did not appear to have inappropriately obtained or extracted sensitive information about its technology or customers. But the cloak-and-dagger details of the case have gained attention in Silicon Valley and in law enforcement and national security circles. “Silicon Valley is ground zero for espionage from a variety of countries around the world,” said Amy Zegart, a professor at Stanford University who specialises in national security and intelligence. She added that she was “troubled” by the OpenAI incident and expected more cases “because these companies are so important.” An OpenAI spokesperson said the company had “a rigorous insider risk program to protect our employees, our intellectual property and customer data” and declined to discuss its monitoring process. Advertisement Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment. His lawyer, William Pernik, said in an email that his client “poses no flight risk whatsoever,” cited his “long-standing ties to the community” and said that he would contest the allegations and detention at a hearing on Monday. “I am aware of the narrative that is being painted,” Pernik said, “and we will fight it wholeheartedly.” In a court filing, prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on September 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. US Department of Justice RAED and the Saudi Embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment. In a filing in US District Court for the Northern District of California, which was unsealed prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on September 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. Only executives and their assistants could reserve the room, which was used for leadership meetings and briefings with government officials, the complaint said. Advertisement OpenAI employees then placed a camera in the conference room, prosecutors said, and it recorded Alfozan checking behind the TV on October 5. That day, security staff found a second device in a bag that Alfozan had left in a printer room, the complaint said. Last month, an AI chatbot account linked to Alfozan’s wife was used to ask how to build a continuous audio recorder, add Wi-Fi connectivity, encrypt its memory card and hide its activity, according to the complaint. Alfozan asked an AI tool to list meeting rooms in OpenAI’s offices and asked about locations for “leadership and exec,” prosecutors said. Alfozan, his wife and another relative had booked one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia for this past Monday, prosecutors said in another court filing. Born in Saudi Arabia’s central region of Qassim and raised in Dammam, Alfozan got into Mawhiba, the kingdom’s national program for gifted students, he said in the interview with “Identity Capital,” an Arabic podcast about professionals and careers. He later received a scholarship through a gifted-student program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. articles.title: Drone Attack Sets Tanker Ablaze Off Romania: Seven Missing
articles.content: Image source, ReutersImage caption, A search and rescue operation involving boats and helicopters is now continuing in rough seas, Romania's authorities say Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say. The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire. Romanian President Nicușor Dan confirmed that the Wine Trader and another chemical tanker in the area, the Yara J, had both been struck by drones - the Yara J on Wednesday. Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port had been hit. It did not name the vessels. Overnight, a swarm of Russian drones was detected not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island. The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing. Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy. A search and rescue operation for the missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed. The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel. The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area. The Wine Trader tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 (05:00 GMT). Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader had been hit by two drones. The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked. This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened. The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state." Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region. The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area. Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable". Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine. A fire broke out on the Comoros-flagged Yara J late on Wednesday after being struck by a drone, but its crew - who are all reportedly safe - were able to douse the flames themselves. Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi. Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports. Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked. Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea. Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Amazon Launches 'Bee' Personal AI Listening Devices
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAmazon is releasing two new Bee listening devices as it moves further into the AI hardware market.The $75 Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of its wearable bracelet, while the $100 Bee Eclipse attaches to a user's smartphone. It marks the first update to the Bee lineup since Amazon acquired the startup in July 2025. In this article Amazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market. The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor. Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations. The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post. Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said. Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware. Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets, while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia-powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI. The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market. Meta has seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers. Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called Muse Charm that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. Plaud developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and Friend offers an AI necklace. Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word. When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions. With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said. An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said.

articles.title: Musk Implies US Government Slowed Starshield in Ukraine
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Both the Starshield system and Starlink system are designed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 15, 2026, 06:45 AM Updated Oct 15, 2026, 09:28 PM Set as preferred source Listen WASHINGTON – SpaceX boss Elon Musk said on Oct 14 that any disruptions reported by Ukraine in using the Starshield satellite communications system would be the responsibility of the US government, not his company. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to US President Donald Trump. Musk drew a distinction between the Starshield system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations. Both were designed by Musk’s SpaceX. Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that “Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160kmh is being restored”, but that “removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defence”. Fedorov then thanked Musk for his “continued support”. Ukrainian defence officials have suggested Washington is behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones. Ukraine has also accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes, with Kyiv hit by ballistic missiles for two nights in a row before air raid sirens could sound to warn people to take cover. Opposition Democrats in the US Senate and House denounced the Trump Administration over the reported interrupted connections. “Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing restrictions as “unconscionable” while Ukraine faced an onslaught of Russian drones and missiles. In the Senate’s Foreign Relations Committee, top Democrat Jeanne Shaheen said the “restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately”, adding that “lives are at stake”. Shaheen also said that the defence department is required to notify “Congress if it pauses or downgrades intelligence sharing with Ukraine”, and called on Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth to immediately provide that notification if there are changes. Republican Senator Tom Tillis also voiced concern, posting on X: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a grey area for the US government or for American corporations.” Trump, facing key midterm elections i n November , in which fuel prices are a major issue, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on supplies and increase in prices at the pump. A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks. Trump denied doing so on Oct 13 . AFP Ukraine Russia Elon Musk SpaceX Wars and conflicts

articles.title: Palm OS Tools Released to GitHub After 25 Years
articles.content: Aaron Ardiri opened his old development archive after discovering enthusiasts were still improving apps for the platform Brandon Vigliarolo Brandon Vigliarolo GOVERNMENT AND IT NEWS REPORTER Published thu 15 Oct 2026 // 21:28 UTC Make us preferred on Google Spies, prime ministers, and balls: The BBC Domesday project @ 40 11 days ago YouTube lunatic designed and 3D printed a working mechanical calculator 15 days ago A 1980s PDP-11 is still running Unix – and now you can watch 22 days ago Apple iPhone Duo makes developers think in folds September 15, 2026 The improbable music of the ZX Spectrum's one-bit speaker September 13, 2026 A small but active community of retro computing enthusiasts is working to keep Palm OS alive, and a developer who recently became aware of their existence has just handed them a treasure trove of code he had no idea was still useful.  Swedish developer Aaron Ardiri published around a gigabyte of Palm OS development resources on GitHub on Thursday in a bid to preserve them for community consumption. Prior to their upload, Ardiri told The Register that the files were languishing in his own personal backups for more than 25 years, preserved only for his own records as part of his past as a developer of Palm OS applications.  “Everything in the archive was accumulated during my years as an active Palm OS developer,” Ardiri explained in an email. “It includes SDKs, technical documentation, conference presentations, development utilities, examples, and some limited system source code that was originally made available to developers to help them understand the operating system's UI and internal components.” One gigabyte of such info might not seem like a lot today, but back in the halcyon era of the PalmPilot, that was a whole heap of valuable data.  Ardiri had previously published source code from his own Palm OS apps on GitHub for those who were interested in it, but he had assumed it was just for public record and that no one would really want to muck about with old Palm OS apps.  “A developer recently submitted a pull request to my original Lemmings source repository, adding HiRes+ display support for the Palm Tungsten T3,” Ardiri explained. “I had no idea people were still actively developing and improving this software more than two decades later.” That sent him down a rabbit hole. He soon realized there were Palm OS enthusiasts on Reddit, Discord, and other online communities all looking for resources to keep their vintage hardware alive and their retro software viable.  “It made me realize that the old development resources sitting on my backup drives might actually be useful to people today,” he said. And now here we are, with a nice, fat GitHub repo full of resources Palm OS users can make use of.  It’s worth noting that just because Ardiri has published this stuff on GitHub, that doesn’t mean it’s open source and ripe for the picking. He’s taken steps to avoid stepping on any copyright toes by leaving out things like Palm OS ROM images, firmware, simulators, and commercial apps that he felt he ought not to distribute as he didn’t have explicit permission. Ardiri sees this as a historical preservation effort, not an attempt to circumvent IP laws.  “A lot of early mobile development knowledge has disappeared with old websites, developer forums, and documentation archives. Some of it survives only in personal collections like mine,” Ardiri told us.  He said that he’s thrilled to have been introduced to the world of Palm enthusiasts, and recently passed off more than 50 old Palm OS devices to Russian dev and Palm OS preservationist Dmitry Grinberg . “This has been an unexpected rediscovery of a period of my career that I thought was largely behind me,” Ardiri told us. “It's clear that Palm OS has a much more active community than I realized … the repository is my contribution to those efforts, providing a historical record of what development looked like when Palm OS was a thriving commercial platform.”  It makes you wonder what other digital gold is sitting in backups just waiting to be discovered. Take this as a sign to take a look through your old drives – you never know what you might find that someone has long been looking for.  ® retro computing mobile offbeat palm Make us preferred on Google

Varonis specializes in data security, mapping where sensitive information sits inside an organization, who can reach it, and how it is actually used. Proofpoint, owned by private equity company Thoma Bravo, built its business around protecting people, blocking phishing, fraud and other attacks that arrive primarily through email and target employees rather than machines. Sumit Dhawan, Proofpoint’s CEO, wrote in a blog post Wednesday that AI is changing the security equation on two fronts. Outside the enterprise, attackers are using AI to launch faster and more advanced campaigns aimed at data and critical systems. Inside, companies are deploying AI agents that have wide-ranging access to sensitive information, creating new categories of insider risk. “Data Security — protecting data from compromise, loss, and misuse by people or AI agents — has become the defining priority for organizations seeking to realize AI’s full potential,” Dhawan wrote. The companies frame the deal as a response to that dual pressure. In a joint announcement, they said the combined organization would serve millions of organizations globally, and described plans for helping organizations adopt and secure AI. Proofpoint’s global reach, he wrote, includes 3.4 million customers, 2.37 trillion emails scanned annually, 410 billion data security events ingested, and more than 13,000 sensors across 105 countries. Those signals feed what the company calls its Knowledge Graph, which strengthens its AI models with intelligence on threats, human behavior and data risk. Combined with Varonis’ visibility into sensitive data, the companies envision a foundation for discovering and remediating risks at machine speed. “For CISOs and CIOs, this also means stronger protection with less complexity and lower costs,” Dhwan wrote. “Our goal is to simplify security operations, enable vendor consolidation, and free up resources for reinvestment in innovation, while maintaining open integrations across the broader cybersecurity ecosystem.” The deal extends a buying pattern for both companies. In February, Proofpoint acquired Acuvity , an AI security startup whose platform monitors how employees and automated systems interact with external AI services. Financial terms were not disclosed.  That purchase followed Proofpoint’s acquisition of Hornetsecurity , a German provider of Microsoft 365 security services, in a deal reportedly worth more than $1 billion. Varonis, for its part, acquired the AI security firm AllTrue.ai for $150 million.  Yaki Faitelson, Varonis’ CEO and co-founder, said the company’s mission is “to secure AI and the data that powers it” and that joining Proofpoint would advance that goal faster than the company could on its own. The deal, approved unanimously by Varonis’ board, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

articles.title: Oncology Emerges as AI's Most Important Proving Ground
articles.content: Innovation By Jackie Njoroge , Forbes Councils Member. for Forbes Technology Council COUNCIL POST Expertise from Forbes Councils members, operated under license. Opinions expressed are those of the author. | Membership (fee-based) Oct 15, 2026, 03:45pm EDT This voice experience is generated by AI. Learn more . This voice experience is generated by AI. Learn more . Jackie Njoroge is VP, Digital Transformation and Operational Excellence at US Oncology . Healthcare is complex. Within healthcare, oncology is even more complex. A patient’s journey starts before the first appointment, with a referral that triggers the movement of records across multiple facilities and systems. By the time a patient sits down with an oncologist, the care team may have already navigated prior authorization and assembled clinical documentation from multiple sources. Then treatment begins, bringing coordination across providers and billing.​ I lead digital transformation and operational excellence for a physician-owned network that includes oncology and several specialty care disciplines. As we leverage technology to help enable better patient outcomes, we find that some of the most impactful AI work we are doing is happening where care is being delivered.​ Where AI Is Already Making a Difference One of the first areas where we focused was ambient scribing. AI tools handle real-time documentation so that after the visit, the provider has an intelligently transcribed record ready for review and doesn’t have to spend significant time compiling notes by hand. The clinician still signs off on every note, but the process takes much less time and effort, so their attention can be entirely on the patient during the appointment. ​ We have also built AI tools for smart preparation before visits. If a provider is seeing 10 patients in a day, they need a concise summary of each patient before walking into the room, one that draws from records across multiple systems. What used to fall on the care team to pull together manually can now happen automatically through AI, giving time back to the care teams.​ Oncology scheduling can be extremely complex: A patient may need labs, then pretreatment steps, then infusions timed precisely relative to what came before. Managing that sequencing manually takes significant effort to ensure patients get the best care possible. Layering AI on top of scheduling systems can help recognize patterns and identify next best actions more efficiently.​ We are building toward a model where a patient calls our contact center, and an agentic AI handles intake and schedules the visit using that same logic. When you have a cancer diagnosis, every day matters. How many days of unnecessary waiting could be eliminated by a scheduling system that sees the entire calendar and sequences automatically?​ AI is also changing how we approach billing and care navigation. The thoughtful use of AI in prior authorization and billing workflows can help streamline administrative processes and reduce the delays and friction patients may face at an already difficult time.​ These solutions don’t just benefit patients; they also help prevent provider burnout. Our providers need to be fully present with a patient who may be having one of the worst days of their life, and anything that simplifies the process helps make that happen.​ Earning Clinician Buy-In How do you build trust in AI broadly, given that AI-generated outputs can sometimes be inaccurate or incomplete and clinicians operate in high-stakes care settings? Rather than asking clinicians to trust any AI tool blindly, you build systems and processes that earn their trust.​ That starts with involving clinicians in building the system. We have strong clinician tech champions who give feedback on our existing workflows and help define what good outputs look like. When we rolled out ambient scribing, early on, some people may have doubted it would ever work. AI systems perform best when they are carefully configured, tested and refined with input from the people who use them. As the industry has matured significantly, and large language models (LLMs) now arrive with substantial base knowledge built in, we have been able to accelerate adoption in a way that is compliant and improves both efficiency and experience. This Is Transformation, Not A Purchase The broader lesson for all of healthcare is this: If you approach AI as a technology purchase, it will underdeliver. This is organizational transformation, meaning you need to start with the business problem. Identify the repeatable tasks where AI can free up human capacity for higher-judgment, more empathetic work. Run small technology/AI options alongside deliberate process design.​ Organizations that spend too long building the perfect plan will find the tools have moved on before they can deploy them. The real goal is a more intelligent and responsive healthcare organization, with providers who have the tools and bandwidth to give the best care possible every day. With thoughtful and careful implementation, AI can help you get there.​​ Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify? articles.title: Chinese Users 'Sell' Faces to AI, Earn Little
articles.content: Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI Companies that let users license their likenesses for use in AI-made short dramas and ads promise high income in a short period. But users report few real financial gains. By Fan Yiying Oct 15, 2026 # technology # artificial intelligence Users in China who “sold their faces,” or licensed their likenesses, for use in AI short dramas and livestreams months ago report receiving few or no requests for their use, and consequently almost no related income. Domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily reported Monday that many users on multiple domestic face-licensing platforms, such as NCAIGC, Mirafans, and ActID, which promise steady income and payment after use of a person’s likeness in their licensing agreements, have not received remuneration. Face-licensing platforms first emerged around May this year, fueled by the growth of AI-generated content, particularly ultrashort dramas . At a September press conference held by the State Council Information Office, it was announced that more than 90% of the 430,000 ultrashort dramas released in China in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated. The platforms attract users by advertising a low barrier to entry and high returns, with claims such as “earn nearly 2,500 yuan ($370) in three days with face selling” going viral on social media, state broadcaster CCTV reported Tuesday. Face licensing lets individuals license their digital likenesses — otherwise protected from use by others under China’s Personal Information Protection Law — to a platform for use in AI ultrashort dramas and ads, among other content. According to CCTV, registration on face-licensing platforms usually requires users to undergo real-name authentication, upload photos of themselves, and set a desired price for each use of their likeness. Some platforms also require users to specify which roles and scenarios they allow companies to use their likenesses for, such as villains, death scenes, or romance. Buyers can select single-use or single-project authorization, and the licensor must accept within 24 hours, after which authorization documents are generated and materials released. Platforms take about a 30% cut.  Regular users can earn about 100 yuan per short video that uses their likeness, with some platforms setting a 500-yuan minimum, while professional actors may reportedly receive up to 10,000 yuan.  Wang Jinlin, a model based in the southern city of Guilin, licensed her face on ActID in May. If a buyer selects her portrait for commercial use, she says they’ll typically offer a one-time payment of 500 to 1,000 yuan. But so far, no studio has asked to use her likeness, she told Sixth Tone. “There are probably few companies making AI live-action short videos right now — there’s no complete pipeline yet,” Wang said. She sees joining the platform as a way to protect her portrait: storing her portrait data should flag unauthorized use, and require any creator to apply for authorization through the platform before using her likeness. That many report never receiving payments after licensing their faces could be because demand for non-celebrity likenesses is low. The head of AI production at a film and television company, surnamed Zheng, told CCTV that companies mainly seek celebrity and short-drama influencer likenesses, leaving little opportunity for regular people. Liu Xiao, founder of ActID, told Southern Metropolis Daily that the platform ultimately provides users with an entry point to be seen and selected by buyers, rather than a contract that guarantees monetization. Criminals may also steal others’ likenesses for AI use rather than go through official channels like face-licensing platforms. On Oct. 8, Beijing’s market regulator warned that lawbreakers tend to scrape selfies, videos, and voices from social platforms and use AI to generate avatars and clone voices from this material for commercial and livestream use.  “Many celebrities cannot fully guarantee their portrait and voice rights, let alone facial licensing in the AI field,” Zheng said. “It’s hard for ordinary people to define how large the gray area (of legal portrait use) is.”  Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson. (Header image: An authorization page on face-licensing platform NCAIGC, Aug. 26, 2026. VCG)

articles.title: Marissa Mayer Warns Against AI Overconfidence
articles.content: Marissa Mayer has been a builder in Silicon Valley since the dawn of Google. But even she says the honest answer about where AI is headed is that nobody knows. Recommended Video “We have a new form of intelligence, and anyone who says they know how this is going to play out is either lying or arrogant or both,” Mayer told Fortune executive editorial director Diane Brady on stage at the annual Most Powerful Women Summit in California, when asked about the debate raging over the frontier AI labs. The uncertainty cuts both ways, said Mayer. “We have to acknowledge that there is a possibility that things won’t go well,” she said. But Mayer put the odds of a negative outcome at “well less than 50%,” noting that even some AI doomers would agree with her. “What that really means is the odds are in our favor,” she said, pointing to potential medical and science breakthroughs and “freeing people up to spend their time and live their lives the way they want to.” She admitted to being an optimist, but welcomed discussions about regulation and collaborations across frontier labs as they advance. She also acknowledged, in responding to a question from Brady, that public sentiment in the U.S. has turned against AI, and she said the industry probably bears some of the blame. The early positioning of the technology was “perhaps too cavalier,” she said, leaving people to question what the enterprise-level embrace of AI will mean for jobs, families, and children’s futures. “I personally think it can make all three of those things better,” she told Brady. Mayer has had a long run at the top of tech, joining Google as an early engineer and becoming one of its most high-profile executives before taking over Yahoo as CEO in 2012, becoming the youngest woman to be a CEO in the Fortune 500 at the time. Accordingly, her tenure drew an intense spotlight, including her decision to take a short maternity leave. Looking back, Mayer said people missed the context. “Yahoo couldn’t afford to have a CEO who was out for three or six months,” she said. Mayer left Yahoo after the sale of its core assets and real estate to Verizon for $4.8 billion in 2017. After Yahoo, she founded contacts and photo-sharing startup Sunshine, before winding it down in 2025 and selling its assets to Dazzle AI. The new startup raised $8 million in a seed round that same year at a $35 million valuation, and formally announced its launch on September 29 this year. Dazzle, the new venture, is a personal AI assistant that learns from the photos on a user’s phone, said Mayer. The idea grew from her work at Sunshine, where Mayer’s team concluded that about 60% of a typical camera roll is worth sharing. The other 40% is “all the stuff we need to get done,” she said, pointing to appointment cards at the dentist’s office and photos of children’s cleats as a reminder to buy a larger size. Dazzle, says Mayer, pairs that context with human and AI agents that can act on it, creating what Mayer described as a to-do list “that gets itself done.” “If I had to be your personal assistant for a week—booking travel, buying gifts, buying clothes, keeping track of kids’ schedules—I’d ask for your camera roll,” she said. As for privacy, Mayer said users can grant Dazzle full, partial, or no access to their photos and images that are sensitive are immediately discarded. For now, Dazzle is invite-only and eventually Mayer said the company will charge subscription fees, transaction fees, or both, but will keep a free tier. One surprise that isn’t all that surprising is that early Dazzle adopters are men, said Mayer, but she said she hoped the product—and AI more broadly—will find a home with women. “I hope that there’s more women that are inspired to actually build,” she said. “I think it’s really important for us to have a voice in how AI develops.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom.
